title: Microbiome-Responsive Hydrogels: From Biological Cues to Smart Biomaterials
content: Stimuli-responsive hydrogels (SRHs) represent a class of “smart” materials engineered to undergo reversible physicochemical transitions in response to abiotic cues such as pH, temperature, ionic strength, redox conditions, and externally applied light, magnetic, or electrical fields. Such responsiveness has enabled clinically relevant applications with several U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved formulations demonstrating translational feasibility. Although these systems have been effective in regulated drug release, wound healing, and tissue engineering, they often lack the ability to respond with true biological specificity. Human tissues, particularly those richly colonized by microbes, have unique microenvironmental features that reflect metabolic behavior, enzymatic secretions, and microorganism communication molecules. These cues are potent endogenous triggers, spatiotemporal and disease-specific, tightly bound to host physiology. Over the past few years, microbiomes have become a central regulator of human health with significant effects on metabolism, immune response, susceptibility to infection, and tissue homeostasis. Microbial communities can cause significant changes in the microenvironment, including local pH gradients, production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), secretion of quorum-sensing molecules, biofilm assembly, and expression of distinct enzymatic profiles, which are not recapitulated in stimuli-responsive materials. The utilization of these microbe-derived cues offers a novel approach for hydrogel design: microbiome-responsive hydrogels (MRHs). These hydrogels exploit microbial metabolic and biochemical responses for inducing swelling, degradation, drug release, antibacterial activity, or structural transformation. Compared with standard SRHs, MRHs have improved physiological relevance, local specificity, and the promise of precision therapy for disease-related microbes. Nevertheless, MRHs are becoming a rapidly developing field that is fragmented and poorly standardized. This review summarizes the engineering of MRHs and discusses biological stimuli, design practices, and biomedical applications, with the most important being translational constraints. These insights collectively showcase the potential of microbiome-triggered systems as an untapped source of materials for next-generation smart biomaterials.
